lessons.title: Total football
lessons.objective: You can explain the Dutch idea of fluid roles.

payload.prompt: What is the core idea of total football?

options.text: Any player can take any role; the team stays balanced

explanation.correct: Right. Total football is about fluid roles where a full-back can become a midfielder and a midfielder can drop to defend.
explanation.incorrect: Total football means any player can fill any role without the team losing its shape. A winger can move into midfield and a full-back can move forward.
explanation.sayThisLine: Total football, everyone rotates.

payload.prompt: Complete the total football story.
payload.template: Total football was made famous by {{team}} and the national team of the {{country}} in the {{decade}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Rinus Michels and Johan Cruyff shaped a Dutch idea in the early 1970s where players swapped positions and the team stayed balanced.
explanation.incorrect: Total football is Dutch, from the early 1970s, linked to Ajax and the 1974 Netherlands World Cup team led by Johan Cruyff.
explanation.sayThisLine: Total football, that's Dutch, from the seventies.

payload.prompt: Match each tactical idea to its description.

pairs.definition: A fluid system where players rotate roles and any player can take any position as the team rebalances.
Players occupy specific zones so the ball carrier always has passing options, with the system, not just individuals.
The initial lineup of defenders, midfielders and forwards (e.g., 4-3-3) that names a system.

explanation.summary: Total football is about rotation and flexibility; positional play is about zones and geometry.
explanation.sayThisLine: They shift into different positions but keep the shape.

statement.speaker: Coach Rudi
statement.text: In this system, a full-back is a midfielder sometimes, a midfielder is a defender sometimes.

payload.question: What system is the coach describing?
payload.translation: The coach is describing total football, where players move into different positions as the team's shape flows.

followUps.line: Do the players know each other's positions well?
followUps.why: Shows you understand the system requires training.

followUps.line: Is it easier to read if everyone stays in their lane?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're unsure, ask if that's how they usually set up.

payload.prompt: A right-back drifts into midfield while a winger covers behind him. Total football?

scene.alt: A team's full-back moves inside to midfield, and a winger drops back to fill the space he left.

explanation.correct: Yes. In total football players swap positions and teammates cover for each other, so the team keeps its balance while the roles change.
explanation.incorrect: Total football is about fluid roles. When a full-back moves inside and someone covers his spot, the team keeps its shape while the positions rotate.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's total football, everyone covers for everyone.

lessons.title: Tiki-taka and positional play
lessons.objective: You can explain tiki-taka and positional play.

payload.prompt: What is tiki-taka?

options.text: Short-passing possession football based on triangles and patient movement

explanation.correct: Right. Tiki-taka is short, quick passing and movement to keep the ball and slowly open a gap. It is linked to Barcelona and Spain around 2008 to 2012, though Guardiola himself disliked the label.
explanation.incorrect: Tiki-taka is a possession style based on short passes and constant movement, made famous by Barcelona and Spain. It is not a formation or a long-ball style.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's tiki-taka, endless passing until the gap opens.

payload.prompt: Positional play means players stay rooted in fixed spots all game. True or false?

scene.alt: A team keeps its players in organised zones while the ball moves, with runners rotating into the spaces.

explanation.correct: False. Positional play asks players to occupy the right zones so the ball carrier always has options, but they still move and rotate when the situation changes.
explanation.incorrect: Positional play is about occupying the right space at the right time, not standing still. Players shift, rotate and re-occupy zones as the ball moves.
explanation.sayThisLine: It isn't standing still, it's about being in the right space.

payload.prompt: Match the tactical concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Rapid, short-pass possession football using triangles; made famous by Barcelona and Spain.
A system where players occupy zones so the ball carrier always has two passing options.
Three players forming a triangle that guarantees the ball carrier two passing options.

explanation.summary: Tiki-taka is a style; positional play is the system; triangles are the geometry that makes both work.
explanation.sayThisLine: Triangles everywhere, they always have an easy pass on.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Spain played that endless passing game, it was hypnotic.

payload.question: What style of play is the fan talking about?
payload.translation: The fan is describing Spain's tiki-taka style: endless short passes that move defenders around until space opens.

followUps.why: Asks about results, not just style.

followUps.line: Do teams still play that way?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you haven't seen it, ask who invented that style.

payload.prompt: Which club is known for modern positional play?

explanation.correct: Yes. Guardiola's Manchester City are a leading example of positional play, occupying zones to create overloads and passing lanes.
explanation.incorrect: Guardiola's teams at Barcelona, Bayern and Manchester City are the best-known modern examples of positional play. Klopp's Liverpool are better known for gegenpressing.
explanation.sayThisLine: City build in a box in midfield, with the full-backs inside.

payload.prompt: Complete the concept.
payload.template: A {{term}} is three players forming a shape that guarantees the ball carrier {{count}} passing options.

explanation.correct: Right. A triangle in passing means you never have only one option.
explanation.incorrect: Three players forming a triangle mean the ball carrier can pass to either of the other two.

lessons.title: Catenaccio
lessons.objective: You can explain the Italian defensive tradition.

payload.prompt: What is catenaccio?

options.text: An Italian defence-first system with a sweeper and strict marking, built to win 1-0

explanation.correct: Correct. Catenaccio is Italian, ultra-defensive, and uses a sweeper behind the defence.
explanation.incorrect: Catenaccio is the original Italian defensive masterclass: a sweeper, marking defenders, and compact shape built to win narrowly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Catenaccio was the original park-the-bus.

payload.prompt: In catenaccio, the sweeper plays behind the back line to clean up. True or false?

scene.alt: A defender stands behind the other defenders, ready to clear loose balls or cover gaps.

explanation.correct: True. The sweeper, or libero, is the extra defender behind the line who tidies up loose balls and covers when someone is beaten.
explanation.incorrect: A sweeper plays behind the rest of the defence, covering through balls and loose clearances. That is why catenaccio was so hard to break down.
explanation.sayThisLine: The sweeper cleans up behind the back line.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive philosophy to its approach.

pairs.definition: An Italian system with a sweeper, strict man-marking, and deep positioning to win 1-0.
Defending deep and compactly, protecting the box and hitting on the counter.
Each defender is responsible for one attacker, following them across the pitch.

explanation.summary: Catenaccio is a specific Italian tradition; low block is a modern compact defence.
explanation.sayThisLine: They parked the bus and nicked one on the break.

statement.speaker: Pundit
statement.text: That team is playing catenaccio, they're never going to open up.

payload.question: What does the pundit mean?

options.text: They have a very defensive, closed setup and will only try to score on the counter
They are too tired to defend

payload.translation: Catenaccio is a defensive system where the team stays compact and organized, defending deep and rarely opening up to attack.

followUps.line: Is that an effective way to play?
followUps.why: Opens a debate about style vs results.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you've never seen it, ask why they chose such a defensive setup.

payload.prompt: Complete the catenaccio idea.
payload.template: Catenaccio is an {{nation}} idea: defend first, because a 1-0 win is {{value}} as a 5-4 win.

explanation.correct: Right. Catenaccio grew in Italian football, and its belief is that three points are three points however you get them.
explanation.incorrect: Catenaccio is Italian and pragmatic: a 1-0 win and a 5-4 win are worth the same three points, so it prioritises not conceding.
explanation.sayThisLine: Winning 1-0 is the same as winning 5-4 on the table.

lessons.title: Gegenpressing
lessons.objective: You can explain why the turnover is the playmaker.

payload.prompt: What is gegenpressing?

options.text: A German term for counter-pressing: immediate pressing after losing the ball
A defensive line holding an offside trap

explanation.correct: Right. Gegenpressing is Klopp's German word for counter-pressing: you win the ball back immediately.
explanation.incorrect: Gegenpressing (counter-pressing) means pressing the opponent right after losing possession, before they can organise.
explanation.sayThisLine: Klopp said gegenpressing is the best playmaker.

payload.prompt: Winning the ball high up the pitch can be as dangerous as a killer pass. True or false?

scene.alt: A team wins the ball near the opponent's penalty area, with the opposition defence not yet set.

explanation.correct: True. This is the gegenpressing idea, where winning the ball near the opponent's goal gives you a chance without a long build-up.
explanation.incorrect: When you win the ball high, the opposing defence is out of shape and you are close to goal. That is why coaches say the turnover can be the best playmaker.
explanation.sayThisLine: Win it high and you're straight on goal.

payload.prompt: Match the pressing concept to its description.

pairs.definition: Pressing immediately after losing the ball to win it back before opponents can organise.
The English term for gegenpressing; same idea of immediate team pressing after turnover.
A cue like a back pass or bad touch that tells the team to press together.

explanation.summary: Gegenpressing and counter-press mean the same thing; a trigger is the signal to do it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The back pass was the trigger and they all went.

statement.speaker: Klopp
statement.text: We win the ball close to their goal and we score within six seconds.

payload.question: What strategy is Klopp describing?

options.text: Patient build-up play from the back
Gegenpressing: winning the ball high and attacking immediately

payload.translation: Klopp is describing gegenpressing: his team presses high, wins the ball, and because they're close to goal, they score quickly.

followUps.line: Does it work in every game?
followUps.why: Shows you understand it has limitations.

followUps.line: What happens if it doesn't work?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you've never heard this, ask if it's a new tactic.

payload.prompt: What is the risk of gegenpressing?

options.text: If pressing fails, the defence is exposed and the attacker is free to counter
The goalkeeper cannot use his hands

explanation.correct: Exactly. If you press and lose the duel, you have space behind you for a quick counter.
explanation.incorrect: The risk is leaving space in defence if the press doesn't win the ball immediately.
explanation.sayThisLine: High press is reward and risk, space behind if you lose it.

payload.prompt: Order a successful counter-press from start to finish.

items.why: The press starts the moment possession changes.

items.text: Nearest players close the ball at once
items.why: Speed matters in the first few seconds while the opponent is not yet organised.

items.text: Teammates cut off the passing lanes
items.why: The press works because the ball carrier has no easy pass.

items.text: Your team wins the ball back
items.why: The opponent is out of shape and you are near the goal.

items.text: You attack before they can reset
items.why: A quick chance is the reward for the risk.

explanation.correct: That is the sequence: lose it, react, cut the lanes, win it and attack before they recover.
explanation.incorrect: The counter-press starts the moment you lose the ball, then the group closes the lanes, wins it back and attacks quickly while the opponent is out of shape.
explanation.sayThisLine: We lost it, swarmed them and scored within seconds.

lessons.title: Inverted full-backs
lessons.objective: You can explain why full-backs move into midfield.

payload.prompt: Tap the area an inverted full-back moves into.

diagram.alt: Overhead view of a full pitch, your team attacking upward. The middle of the pitch is highlighted between the two penalty areas, and each touchline is marked.

explanation.correct: Right. An inverted full-back steps inside from the touchline into central midfield to give the team an extra body in the middle.
explanation.incorrect: A traditional full-back stays wide on the touchline. An inverted full-back tucks inside into central midfield.
explanation.sayThisLine: The right-back tucks inside, he's an inverted full-back.

payload.prompt: What does it mean for a full-back to invert into midfield?

options.text: Move from the wing into central midfield when the team has the ball
Play in a different position every five minutes

explanation.correct: Correct. The full-back steps inside from the flank to add a body in midfield.
explanation.incorrect: An inverted full-back tucking inside means moving from the touchline into the centre of midfield.
explanation.sayThisLine: The right-back tucks inside, he's an inverted full-back.

payload.prompt: Complete the inverted full-back idea.
payload.template: An inverted full-back steps {{direction}} from the flank into midfield, giving his team an extra {{player}} there.

explanation.correct: Right. Stepping inside adds a player to central midfield, creating an overload and more passing options.
explanation.incorrect: An inverted full-back moves inside from the flank, adding a body in midfield so his team can win the middle and keep the ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: It gives you an extra body in midfield.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: Manchester City build in a box in midfield, with the full-backs inside.

payload.question: What formation concept is the analyst describing?

options.text: Inverted full-backs creating a box shape with midfielders

payload.translation: The analyst is describing a box midfield where Guardiola's full-backs step inside to form a compact shape with the midfielders.

followUps.line: Does that leave the flanks empty?
Who fills the wide spaces then?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're unsure, ask how the full-backs can play in midfield.

payload.prompt: Match the role to its function.

pairs.definition: A full-back who steps into midfield to overload the centre and create passing angles.
A build-up shape where full-backs move inside to form a box with central midfielders.
A defender who stays on the flank to cover the wing and overlap to attack.

explanation.summary: Inverted full-backs are modern; they step inside. Traditional full-backs stay wide.
explanation.sayThisLine: They shift inside to control the middle.

lessons.title: Direct football
lessons.objective: You can defend and criticise direct football.

payload.prompt: What is direct football?

options.text: Long passes and target men; using second balls and set pieces

explanation.correct: Right. Direct football goes long early, using target men and set-piece opportunities.
explanation.incorrect: Direct football is a style that plays long balls quickly, relying on target men to flick it on and second balls.
explanation.sayThisLine: They play direct, a lot of long balls and second balls.

payload.prompt: A flick-on drops loose between players. Is that the second ball?

scene.alt: A long ball is headed on by a target man and lands loose between attackers and defenders.

explanation.correct: Yes. The first ball is the long delivery or clearance. The loose ball that drops after a flick-on or header is the second ball.
explanation.incorrect: The second ball is the loose ball after the first contact. Teams built on direct football aim to win these scraps.
explanation.sayThisLine: Win the first ball, then attack the second.

payload.prompt: Match the direct-football concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Playing long balls early to target men, using set pieces and second balls for chances.
The loose ball after a clearance or header; winning it in a set-piece situation often leads to a goal.
A tall striker or midfielder who receives long balls and flicks them on for teammates.

explanation.summary: Direct football relies on target men winning first balls and teammates attacking the second ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: First ball to the target man, second ball to the goal.

statement.speaker: Pundit
statement.text: That's not pretty, but it works. They just go long and fight for scraps.

payload.question: What does the pundit mean by that approach?

options.text: Direct football: long balls, target men, and second-ball chaos

payload.translation: The pundit acknowledges direct football is effective but ungraceful: it bypasses build-up and relies on physical and set-piece battles.

followUps.line: Do elite teams play that way?
followUps.why: Opens a debate about whether it's limiting.

followUps.line: Is it boring or is it smart?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're unsure, ask if that's an easy tactic to defend against.

payload.prompt: A high press is closing in on your keeper. Short or long?

situation.narrative: Your team is 1-0 up, and the opponents are pressing your defenders hard whenever you pass out from the back.

facts.label: Risk
facts.value: A short pass could be intercepted near goal

options.label: Go long to the target striker and fight for the second ball
options.consequence: You skip the press, and the striker can win the flick-on or keep them pinned back.
considerations: Reduces the risk of a turnover near your goal

options.label: Keep playing short passes under pressure
options.consequence: It can pull the press out of shape if it works, but a slip near your own goal could cost you the lead.
considerations: Rewarded if your players are calm
High risk with a lead to protect

options.label: Boot it out of play every time
options.consequence: You give the ball away and the pressure comes straight back, with no plan for the second ball.

payload.expertNote: Direct football is not just about being ugly. Against a strong press, a long ball to a target man can be a smart way to skip the pressure and win territory, as long as the team is organised for the second ball.
payload.sayThisLine: Sometimes going long is the clever choice.

lessons.title: Style vs results
lessons.objective: You can talk about the beauty-versus-results debate without taking a cheap side.

payload.prompt: What is the style vs results debate?

options.text: Attractive possession football versus winning-first pragmatism
Whether defenders or strikers matter more

explanation.correct: Right. Some fans want beautiful football; others just want wins. Both are valid.
explanation.incorrect: The debate is between idealists who love possession and attacking flair, and pragmatists who prefer ugly wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: Is it winning ugly or is it pragmatism?

payload.prompt: A pragmatist says three points from a 1-0 are worth the same as from a 5-4. True or false?

scene.alt: Two teams each win their match and both receive the full three points, one by 1-0 and one by 5-4.

explanation.correct: True. The table treats both wins the same, and a pragmatist points to that. An idealist might still argue how you win matters too.
explanation.incorrect: A win is worth three points however it looks. That is the pragmatist's point, though idealists say style matters for enjoyment and long-term success.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three points is three points.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: They play beautiful football but they keep losing. I'd rather win boring.

payload.question: What is this fan's priority?

options.text: Results over style; pragmatism over idealism

payload.translation: The fan is prioritizing wins over entertainment; they'd take a pragmatic, functional approach over beautiful but ineffective play.

followUps.line: Do you agree with that view?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're unsure, ask what matters more: winning or how you win.

payload.prompt: Complete the false-nine idea.
payload.template: A false nine is a {{role}} who drops {{where}} to pull defenders out of position.

explanation.correct: Right. A false nine looks like a striker but drops into midfield, pulling the centre-backs with him or leaving space for runners.
explanation.incorrect: A false nine is a centre-forward who drops deep into midfield. If defenders follow, space opens behind them; if not, he gets time on the ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: He plays as a false nine, so he's always dropping in.

payload.prompt: Match the football philosophy to its approach.

pairs.definition: Valuing beautiful, attacking, possession-based football above results.
Valuing wins and results above style; using whatever works, even if it's ugly.
A striker who drops deep, blending attacking and creative play in an unconventional role.

explanation.summary: Idealists want beautiful football; pragmatists want results. False nine is a way to blend both.
explanation.sayThisLine: Different teams have different philosophies.

exchanges.theirMessage: I hate watching this team. They park the bus and bore everyone.

replies.text: Fair, but boring wins still get you up the table.
replies.theirResponse: I guess results are results, but where's the fun?
replies.coachNote: Acknowledges her frustration and offers a pragmatic counter.

replies.text: Have you seen their xG? They do create chances.
replies.theirResponse: Maybe, but it doesn't look like it.
replies.coachNote: Data helps but it does not replace how the match feels.

replies.text: I get it. Some fans care about winning, others about how.
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. Give me beauty and results, not one or the other.

exchanges.theirMessage: Their new manager plays total football, but we're not winning.

replies.text: It takes time to change a system. Maybe by next season?
replies.theirResponse: I hope so. I want to see it click.
replies.coachNote: Offers patience without dismissing her concern.

replies.text: Do you think the players fit that style?
replies.coachNote: A thoughtful question invites her own analysis.

replies.text: It's frustrating when it looks good but the results don't come.
replies.theirResponse: Right. I know it's a process.
replies.coachNote: Empathises with the tension without taking a side.

payload.title: Bored by the bus
payload.setting: Your friend is frustrated with how her team plays.
payload.closingNote: The style-versus-results debate has no cheap winner. Curious questions keep the conversation open and warm.
